extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary biography; students and scholars of Romantic-era literature
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from a biographical/literary-critical supplement on Coleridge and Lamb, describing childhood, temperament, reading habits, aesthetic tendencies, and critical character. Useful for understanding qualities valued in Romantic-era writers and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of imaginative reading for children
rubrics_metrics.description: Ought children to be permitted to read romances and stories of giants, magicians, and genii? — the author answers affirmatively: such reading is the best way of giving the mind a love of the Great and the Whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/nuance: The page argues that early exposure to the 'Vast' trains the imagination and that sense-experience alone makes the mind focus on little things. Caveat: the author acknowledges critics' warnings that this method may make the mind credulous and prone to superstition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and poetic force may outstrip language
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetic force and originality of an ode (example: Coleridge's Greek Ode) may be 'much beyond the language in which they were conveyed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Evaluate work not only by linguistic polish but by the underlying imaginative force and originality; strong poetic conception can transcend imperfect expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance of moral evil in books as a critical posture
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic/writer may display 'toleration of moral evil' in books: discovering 'the soul of goodness in things evil' and thereby allowing surrounding evil to 'disappear' from mental vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: This is presented as a sympathetic critical stance (exemplified in Charles Lamb) — rather than condemning works for their moral failings, a critic may emphasize redeeming qualities, pity, and tenderness. Not an endorsement of moral laxity, but an approach for reading and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing light and darkness in literary treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred aesthetic tendency described: 'ever introducing streaks and gleams of light into darkness, rather than drowning certain objects in floods of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Writers should consider tempering idealization and also avoid total darkness; the careful insertion of hope or gentleness amid flaw yields a humane portrayal. This balance stems from indulgence toward human nature rather than indifference to evil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of exaltation and severe character analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable literary quality is the coexistence of a power to exalt/glorify with a power of severe analysis and poignant exhibition of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: The passage holds this combination up as rare and powerful — the ability to admire warmly while also performing incisive, sometimes painful, character study is a mark of major talent (and may create personal conflict for the writer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative value of wide, even desultory, reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading broadly (even 'whether I understood them, or did not') from an early age fosters imaginative development and a continual inner life; this habit is linked to prodigious book-knowledge and creative fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Encourages permissive access to books and folios for young readers; implies that curiosity-driven, even unsystematic reading contributes to a writer's inner resources. Implicit caution: such immersion can be coupled with poor physical health or social costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personal temperament and experience in poetic conception
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's natural temperament (joyous, day-dreaming, imaginative) and formative experiences (childhood solitude, library access, school discipline) shape their poetic faculty — e.g., producing continuous 'low fever' of creative absorption and unique imaginative output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: When evaluating creative work, consider biographical/temperamental sources of imaginative intensity; formative hardships or oddities may be interpreted as contributing to creative power rather than mere pathology.
